abstract: |
  Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 does more than replace Directive 2006/42/EC with a directly applicable machinery regulation. It extends the machinery-safety model into the digital mechanisms through which modern machines can be configured, connected, updated, remotely controlled, and intentionally manipulated. This article examines the Regulation's general legal changes and then focuses on its treatment of software, digital safety components, substantial modification, protection against corruption, malicious third-party attempts, communication-network failures, self-evolving behaviour, remote maintenance, and safety-related control systems. It distinguishes explicit legal requirements from engineering measures that may be used to satisfy them, analyses the role of functional-safety standards and IEC 62443, and places the Machinery Regulation alongside the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2, and the AI Act. The central question is whether Regulation 2023/1230 changes the boundary of machinery safety itself: when software, connectivity, or external control authority can alter physical behaviour, protecting the integrity of the digital control system becomes part of preventing physical harm.

## The Machinery Regulation changes the boundary of machine safety

**Regulation (EU) 2023/1230** is not simply a recast of Directive 2006/42/EC. It preserves the classical machinery-safety model—risk assessment, inherently safe design, safeguards, safety-related control systems and information for use—but extends that model to the digital mechanisms through which machine behaviour can now be changed. The Commission itself describes the Regulation as integrating provisions for “cyber-safety” concerning compliance-relevant software, data and safety control systems. The decisive legal provisions are Annex III §1.1.9, **Protection against corruption**, and §1.2.1, **Safety and reliability of control systems**. They require protection against intentional as well as accidental corruption and explicitly require control systems, where relevant to the circumstances and risks, to withstand reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts by third parties that could produce a hazardous situation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-001]

That supports the central thesis of this research, but with an important boundary condition:

> **The Machinery Regulation does move machine safety toward cyber-physical safety, but it does not create a general-purpose OT cybersecurity regime. Cybersecurity becomes a machinery-safety requirement when compromise of a digital asset, communication path, software state, configuration or control authority can contribute to a hazardous physical state.**

Consequently, a vulnerability that exposes confidential production data may be important under the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2 or company policy without necessarily violating a machinery EHSR. The same vulnerability becomes directly relevant to Regulation 2023/1230 if it enables an attacker to alter a safety parameter, inhibit a stop, trigger motion, defeat a protective function, corrupt safety-related data or otherwise cause a hazardous situation. That distinction follows from the safety-conditioned language of Annex III rather than from a generic requirement that every machine attain some undefined level of “cybersecurity”. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-002]

## The Directive becomes a Regulation: the legal baseline and the 2027 cut-over

Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 was adopted on 14 June 2023 and replaces Directive 2006/42/EC. Following a corrigendum concerning its dates of application, its main product requirements become mandatory on **20 January 2027**. Machinery first placed on the EU market before that date remains subject to Directive 2006/42/EC; the Commission expressly states that all machinery placed on the market before 20 January 2027 must comply with the Directive, although manufacturers may additionally state conformity with the Regulation where applicable. The Regulation is already in force as EU law, while different provisions on institutional machinery, delegated powers, notified bodies and penalties have phased in at different dates under Article 54. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-003]

The choice of a **Regulation rather than another Directive is substantive in institutional terms**. A Regulation applies directly and does not require each Member State to transpose its product rules into national legislation. The Commission identifies increased legal certainty through uniform application as one of the reasons and also notes alignment with the EU New Legislative Framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-004]

The basic product-safety architecture nevertheless remains familiar. The Regulation sets mandatory essential health and safety requirements; harmonised standards remain voluntary technical means for obtaining presumption of conformity where their references are published in the Official Journal. It also aligns machinery law more closely with the New Legislative Framework by formalising obligations across manufacturers, authorised representatives, importers and distributors and by integrating modern market-surveillance concepts. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-005]

### Scope and definitions

**Scope.** Article 2 covers machinery and what the Regulation calls related products: interchangeable equipment, safety components, lifting accessories, chains, ropes and webbing, and removable mechanical transmission devices; it separately regulates partly completed machinery. Important exclusions remain for, among other things, certain nuclear applications, weapons, specially designed military or police machinery, certain research equipment, mine winding gear, seagoing vessels and mobile offshore units, categories covered by vehicle legislation, and specified electrical/electronic equipment governed through other Union product regimes. The legal perimeter therefore still has to be determined product by product rather than by assuming that every automated industrial asset is “machinery”. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-006]

There are, however, several digital changes in the definitions themselves. The machinery definition expressly accommodates assemblies that are complete except for the upload of software intended for the manufacturer's specific application. More importantly, Article 3 makes a **safety component capable of being a physical or digital component, including software**, when it is independently placed on the market to fulfil a safety function and its failure or malfunction would endanger persons. Software can therefore be a regulated safety product rather than merely documentation accompanying hardware. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-007]

Partly completed machinery remains an assembly that is almost machinery but cannot itself perform the specific application and is intended for incorporation into or assembly with other machinery or equipment. Its manufacturer does not issue the same final machinery EU declaration of conformity; the relevant regime includes technical documentation, assembly instructions and an EU declaration of incorporation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-008]

### Directive 2006/42/EC versus Regulation 2023/1230

The transition from the Directive can be summarised as follows.

| Topic | Directive 2006/42/EC | Regulation 2023/1230 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Legal instrument | Directive requiring national transposition. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-009] | Directly applicable Regulation; main application 20 January 2027. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-010] | **Structural change** |
| Economic operators | Manufacturer-centred model, with authorised representative and supply-chain duties distributed through EU product law. | Explicit NLF-style manufacturer, importer and distributor responsibilities, traceability and corrective-action duties. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-011] | **Clarification/modernisation with practical consequences** |
| Safety components | Predominantly understood through physical machinery components. | Definition explicitly includes **digital components, including software**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-012] | **Substantive digital change** |
| Substantial modification | The Commission's Directive guidance treated sufficiently modified machinery as effectively new machinery, but the Directive lacked the Regulation's explicit horizontal definition. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-013] | Article 3(16) expressly covers modification by **physical or digital means**; Article 18 can make the modifier the manufacturer. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-014] | **Substantive legal clarification** |
| Cybersecurity | No equivalent horizontal requirement explicitly addressing intentional corruption or malicious third-party attacks. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-015] | Annex III §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1 explicitly address intentional corruption and reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-016] | **Major substantive change** |
| Communication networks | Traditional electrical/control-system failure requirements. | Annex III §1.2.6 explicitly extends failure analysis to the **communication network connection**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-017] | **Substantive digital extension** |
| Software traceability | Software faults were already relevant to control-system safety. | Explicit safe-software identification, intervention evidence and safety-software version tracing. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-018] | **Substantive change** |
| AI/adaptive behaviour | No dedicated self-evolving machinery framework. | Requirements for fully/partially self-evolving behaviour, ML-based safety functions and safety-decision records. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-019] | **Substantive change** |
| Remote/autonomous machinery | Remote-controlled mobile machinery was not wholly new as a concept. | Autonomous behaviour is addressed more systematically and now sits beneath horizontal digital-integrity/cyber-safety EHSRs. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-020] | **Mixed: continuity plus expansion** |
| Instructions | Predominantly paper-era model. | Digital instructions and declarations are expressly accommodated subject to conditions and availability safeguards. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-021] | **Modernisation** |
| Technical documentation | Conventional design/risk/test documentation. | Digital evidence becomes more important; Annex IV can require safety-related source code or programming logic to demonstrate conformity upon a reasoned authority request where other documentation is insufficient. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-022] | **Substantive compliance change** |
| Conformity assessment | Annex IV “high-risk” categories under Directive procedures. | Annex I Part A/Part B structure; Part A mandates third-party routes and includes ML-based safety-function categories. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-023] | **Substantive reorganisation** |
| Market surveillance | Established machinery market-surveillance structure. | NLF-aligned duties, explicit economic-operator responsibilities and modern EU market-surveillance framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-024] | **Modernisation/strengthening** |

: Directive 2006/42/EC and Regulation (EU) 2023/1230: principal structural and substantive differences. {#tbl-directive-regulation-comparison}

### Conformity assessment and harmonised standards

The **conformity-assessment distinction in Annex I is particularly important**. Part A contains machinery/products for which a notified-body route is mandatory; it includes safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine-learning approaches that ensure safety functions, and machinery embedding such systems where the systems have not been independently placed on the market. Part B contains additional machinery categories for which internal production control remains available only under the Regulation's conditions concerning harmonised standards or common specifications; otherwise a notified-body route is required. Article 25 establishes the applicable procedures. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-025]

The Regulation does not abolish the harmonised-standard model. Article 20 provides the machinery presumption-of-conformity mechanism, supplemented by common specifications in defined circumstances. There is also a specific bridge to EU cybersecurity certification: where a cybersecurity certification scheme adopted under the Cybersecurity Act is appropriately referenced and covers the relevant requirements, it can support presumption of conformity for the protection-against-corruption/control-system requirements within the limits specified by the Regulation. That is very different from saying that any commercial “IEC 62443 certificate” automatically proves Machinery Regulation compliance. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-026]

A significant current-status point is easily missed. **As of 23 September 2026, the Commission has not yet published the first harmonised-standard list under Regulation 2023/1230.** The Commission's machinery standardisation page says that the vast majority of standards currently cited under Directive 2006/42/EC are expected to feature in the new list, with limitations where they do not fully address new EHSRs, and that the first Machinery Regulation list is expected before the end of 2026. The Directive list itself was most recently amended on 4 September 2026. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-027]

This matters for cyber compliance because **prEN 50742, “Safety of machinery — Protection against corruption”, is still a draft**: DIN Media records the prEN 50742:2025 text as DIN EN 50742:2026-03 Draft, issued in February 2026. It therefore cannot currently be presented as a final harmonised standard conferring a Machinery Regulation presumption of conformity. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-028]

## The machine is now partly software

The most consequential provisions are not hidden in a recital about cybersecurity. They are requirements in **Annex III**, meaning they become part of the safety case against which machinery conformity is assessed.

### Explicit digital requirements

The following table separates what the law actually says from the engineering response that may be reasonable.

| Legal provision | Regulatory requirement | Engineering meaning | Cybersecurity status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Article 3 — safety component** | A safety component can be physical or digital, including software, where the statutory conditions are met. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-029] | Safety software can itself fall inside the machinery product-compliance perimeter. | **Explicit** |
| **Article 3(16) — substantial modification** | Modification may be made by **physical or digital means** after market placement/putting into service. The remaining statutory safety/risk conditions must also be satisfied. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-030] | PLC logic, firmware, software configuration or remote-function changes cannot be dismissed merely because “nothing mechanical changed”. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — connection** | Connection of another device, including through a remote device communicating with the machinery, must not lead to a hazardous situation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-031] | Every control-capable communication path needs a safety consequence analysis. | **Explicit cyber-physical requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — hardware** | Hardware transmitting signals/data relevant to access to compliance-critical software must be adequately protected against accidental or intentional corruption, with evidence of intervention collected where relevant. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-032] | Controller interfaces, engineering ports, gateways and update paths become part of the safety trust boundary. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — software/data** | Software and data critical to EHSR compliance must be identified and adequately protected against accidental or intentional corruption. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-033] | Safety logic, configuration, safe-speed values, interlock mappings and integrity-critical datasets need protection. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — software identity** | The machine must identify software installed on it that is necessary for safe operation and make that information accessible. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-034] | Software/firmware version inventory ceases to be merely an IT asset-management convenience. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.1.9 — intervention evidence** | Machinery must collect evidence of legitimate or illegitimate software intervention or modification of installed software/configuration. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-035] | Auditability/tamper evidence is required; a particular SIEM technology is not. | **Explicit logging/evidence obligation** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(a)** | Control systems must, where appropriate to circumstances and risks, withstand intended/unintended external influences including **reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts from third parties leading to a hazardous situation**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-036] | Threat modelling becomes relevant to the machinery safety case whenever an attacker can influence hazard controls. | **Explicit cybersecurity requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(d)** | Limits of safety functions are established through risk assessment; changes to settings/rules, including during learning, must not create hazardous situations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-037] | Adaptive algorithms cannot be allowed to learn their way outside the validated safety envelope. | **Explicit; cyber controls may be one implementation** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1(f)** | Traceability of interventions and uploaded safety-software versions is to be enabled and retained for the prescribed period, including a five-year traceability requirement tied to safety-software uploads. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-038] | Version provenance and change history need to survive commissioning and service. | **Explicit** |
| **Annex III §1.2.1 — self-evolving systems** | Systems with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour/logic and varying autonomy must remain within defined task/movement boundaries and retain prescribed safety-decision information. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-039] | Runtime adaptation requires bounded authority and retrospective evidence. | **Explicit AI/autonomy requirement** |
| **Annex III §1.2.6** | Interruption, restoration or fluctuation of the power supply **or communication network connection** must not produce hazardous situations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-040] | Loss-of-network, packet loss, reconnection and stale/replayed command conditions require safe-state analysis. | **Explicit digital-safety requirement** |
| **Annex IV technical documentation** | Safety-related source code or programming logic may have to be provided to a competent authority following a reasoned request where normal documentation is insufficient to demonstrate conformity. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-041] | “The PLC code is proprietary” is not an absolute answer to a conformity investigation. | **Explicit compliance-evidence rule** |
| **Article 10 — instructions** | Manufacturers may use digital instructions subject to accessibility, availability and paper-safety-information conditions, particularly for non-professional users. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-042] | Documentation lifecycle and digital availability become product-compliance design questions. | **Digital modernisation, not cybersecurity per se** |

: Digital and cyber-relevant provisions of Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and their engineering significance. {#tbl-digital-requirements}

A particularly important distinction emerges from §1.1.9. The Regulation does **not** prescribe a particular authentication protocol, firewall brand, cryptographic algorithm, secure-boot technology, MFA system, SBOM format or network topology. It states the safety objective: compliance-critical hardware, software and data must be protected against accidental and intentional corruption; connections must not create hazards; and interventions must leave evidence. Controls such as cryptographic firmware signing, role-based access, authenticated engineering sessions and configuration integrity checking are therefore **possible engineering means of satisfying the requirement**, not the literal requirement itself. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-043]

That distinction matters legally. A machine manufacturer should be able to produce a chain of reasoning of the form:

**EHSR → identified cyber-physical hazard → security/safety requirement → chosen control → verification evidence**

rather than:

**EHSR → “we use IEC 62443” → assumed conformity.**

The latter skips the actual machinery risk assessment.

### Substantial modification by digital means

**Substantial modification is the other major digital change.** Article 3(16) expressly recognises modification “by physical or digital means”. But the term has a narrower legal meaning than “significant software change”. The modification must be made after market placement/putting into service, not be foreseen or planned by the original manufacturer, affect machinery safety by creating a new hazard or increasing an existing risk, and meet the further protective-measure conditions set out in the definition. Article 18 then provides that the natural or legal person carrying out such a substantial modification is considered a manufacturer for the purposes of the Regulation and assumes the corresponding obligations. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-044]

That produces very different answers for superficially similar digital changes:

| Change | Likely treatment under the Article 3(16) test |
|---|---|
| Manufacturer-planned cybersecurity firmware update, installed through the validated update process, with no change to the safety envelope | **Normally not substantial merely because it changes code.** It was foreseen and does not necessarily create/increase a hazard. Compliance and configuration evidence still matter. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-045] |
| HMI bug fix with no influence on safety functions or control authority | Usually outside the substantial-modification test, assuming the risk assessment confirms no safety impact. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-046] |
| Integrator modifies PLC/safety PLC logic so an interlocked guard can be opened during a new automatic mode and additional safeguarding or safety-control changes are required | Strong candidate for a substantial modification; Article 18 may make the integrator the manufacturer of the affected machinery. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-047] |
| Addition of permanent remote-control functionality not envisaged by the OEM, enabling machine motion from outside the original operator location | Not automatically substantial, but it may satisfy the test if it creates/increases risk and necessitates the statutory protective measures. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-048] |
| Cloud optimisation sends only recommendations that are validated and bounded by existing local safety/control limits | The presence of cloud software is not enough; the safety effect must be evaluated against Article 3(16). [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-049] |
| Cloud optimisation receives unrestricted write authority over speeds, trajectories or safety-relevant parameters | Much more likely to change the hazard/control model; whether it legally crosses the substantial-modification threshold still depends on the complete statutory test. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-050] |

: Examples illustrating how Article 3(16) may apply to digital modifications. {#tbl-substantial-modification-examples}

The practical lesson is that **“digital modification” and “substantial modification” are not synonyms**. Conversely, “we only changed software” is no longer a viable categorical argument against the possibility of substantial modification. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-051]

## When a cyberattack becomes a machinery-safety event

The Regulation's cyber provisions become easier to understand if the problem is represented as a causal chain rather than as a list of IT controls:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-cyber-physical-causal-chain
%%| fig-cap: "Cyber-physical causal chain from a digital compromise to physical harm."
%%| fig-alt: "A left-to-right causal chain in which a cyber threat compromises a digital asset, alters data, logic, configuration or control authority, produces an unsafe control action or inhibits a safety action, creates a hazardous machine state, exposes a person and may result in harm."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[Cyber threat] --> B[Compromise of a digital asset]
    B --> C[Alteration of data, logic, configuration<br/>or control authority]
    C --> D[Unsafe control action<br/>or inhibited safety action]
    D --> E[Hazardous machine state]
    E --> F[Exposure of a person]
    F --> G[Harm]
```

The Machinery Regulation is primarily interested in the part of this chain from compromised digital state to **hazardous physical behaviour**. Annex III §1.1.9 attacks integrity and unauthorised intervention at the asset/interface level; §1.2.1 attacks the ability of malicious external influence to defeat the control system; §1.2.6 addresses the hazardous consequences of communications failure. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-052]

### Cyber-physical threat scenarios

This produces a useful threat model for industrial machinery.

| Threat scenario | Security consequence | Possible safety consequence | Principal Machinery Regulation hook |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stolen vendor credentials give an attacker engineering access to a PLC | Unauthorised logic/configuration modification | Unexpected motion or removal of safe sequencing | Annex III §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-053] |
| Safety PLC password/account compromised | Modification of safety logic or parameters | Guard bypass, incorrect safe-speed limit, defeated stop function | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| HMI compromised and command channel permits remote start | Control authority captured | Person exposed to unexpected start | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Network injection changes VFD speed/torque command | Command integrity lost | Speed/force exceeds assumptions underlying risk reduction | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| OPC UA credentials permit writes to safety-relevant tags | Authorised protocol used by unauthorised actor | Safety envelope/setpoint altered | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Manipulated sensor values | State estimation corrupted | Controller fails to detect person, obstruction or unsafe position | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Malicious firmware update to drive/controller | Trusted execution base corrupted | STO/safe-motion or braking assumptions invalidated | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Remote gateway compromise | New privileged path to internal controls | Any downstream unsafe control action enabled by the path | §§1.1.9, 1.2.1 |
| Network outage/reconnection creates stale or replayed command | Communications state loses integrity/availability | Unexpected restart, uncontrolled parameter change or inability to stop | §1.2.6 [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-054] |
| ML safety component poisoned or its parameters maliciously altered | Learned decision boundary changed | Safety decisions depart from validated limits | §1.2.1 and AI/ML provisions [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-055] |
| Production historian exfiltrated, with no ability to affect machine control | Confidentiality loss | No necessary physical safety effect | Possibly CRA/NIS2 issue; **not automatically an MR EHSR failure**. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-056] |

: Cyber-physical threat scenarios and the Machinery Regulation provisions they may implicate. {#tbl-cyber-physical-threat-scenarios}

This is why the expression **cyber-physical safety** is useful. It does not mean that safety and security have become identical. It means the independence assumption between the two domains is no longer defensible when security compromise can invalidate a safety assumption.

### Functional safety meets adversarial behaviour

Traditional machinery risk engineering remains indispensable. ISO 12100 specifies machinery risk assessment and risk reduction across relevant lifecycle phases; ISO 13849-1:2023 addresses the design and integration of safety-related parts of control systems, including software; IEC 62061:2021 addresses design, integration and validation of machinery safety-related control systems and is a machinery-sector implementation within the IEC 61508 framework. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-057]

What changes is the **failure model**. Performance Level or SIL reasoning can establish how a safety function tolerates defined random and systematic failures, but an adversary can intentionally select inputs, credentials, configuration pathways and timing to defeat assumptions shared across otherwise independent protection layers. A safety PLC with an excellent dangerous-failure probability does not solve the problem if an attacker can legitimately authenticate with a stolen engineering account and upload a hazardous configuration.

IEC itself now makes the relationship explicit in **IEC TS 63074:2023, “Safety of machinery — Security aspects related to functional safety of safety-related control systems.”** The specification identifies IEC 62443 security threats and vulnerabilities that can lead to loss of the ability of a machinery safety-related control system to maintain safe operation and explicitly includes threat modelling in its scope. That is powerful evidence that functional safety and cybersecurity are distinct engineering disciplines whose risk models have to meet at the safety-related control system. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-058]

The risk-assessment implication can therefore be derived without overreading the Regulation:

1. Annex III §1.2.1 explicitly introduces reasonably foreseeable malicious third-party attempts into the control-system safety requirement. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-059]  
2. ISO 12100 requires identification and assessment of machinery hazards and risk reduction. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-060]  
3. IEC TS 63074 demonstrates that security threats/vulnerabilities can cause loss of machinery safety-control capability. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-061]  
4. Therefore, **where cyber compromise can defeat a risk-reduction measure or produce a hazardous state, the cyber pathway has to enter the machine safety analysis.**

That does not require calculating a SIL for “hacking”. It requires determining which cyber events can invalidate safety functions and ensuring that the machine architecture prevents, constrains or safely handles those events.

The most useful design question becomes:

> **What must an attacker be able to alter before this machine can hurt somebody?**

The answer identifies the machine's **safety-security trust boundary**: safety PLC logic, safety parameters, safe-motion configuration, firmware authenticity, interlock mapping, authorised modes, control ownership, sensor trust, update mechanisms and the communication paths capable of changing them.

## From connected machine to defensible architecture

### IEC 62443 as an engineering implementation framework

IEC 62443 is currently the strongest general engineering framework for translating that trust boundary into industrial cybersecurity architecture, but it must be used with the correct legal status. The IEC describes the 62443 series as addressing security of industrial automation and control systems throughout their lifecycle. IEC 62443-3-2 addresses system security risk assessment and zones/conduits; IEC 62443-3-3 provides system security requirements; IEC 62443-4-1 specifies a secure product-development lifecycle; and IEC 62443-4-2 specifies technical security requirements for IACS components. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-062]

**IEC 62443 is not made mandatory by Regulation 2023/1230**, nor, as of 23 September 2026, is there an MR harmonisation decision making the series a blanket presumption-of-conformity route for Annex III §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1. The first Machinery Regulation harmonised-standard list is still being prepared. prEN 50742 is the more machinery-specific standardisation work explicitly entitled “Protection against corruption”, but it is still a draft. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-063]

The correct relationship is therefore:

**Machinery Regulation = required safety outcome**

**IEC 62443 = useful engineering mechanism for achieving and evidencing parts of that outcome**

not:

**IEC 62443 certificate = automatic Machinery Regulation compliance.**

A practical mapping looks like this.

| Machinery concern | Useful IEC 62443 engineering layer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Identify malicious paths capable of changing machine state | **62443-3-2** | System-under-consideration analysis, zones/conduits and cybersecurity risk assessment. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-064] |
| Prevent unauthorised users/devices controlling machinery | **62443-3-3 / 4-2: Identification & Authentication Control, Use Control** | Authentication and authorisation support protection of safety-relevant access paths. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-065] |
| Prevent corruption of software/configuration | **System Integrity** in 3-3/4-2 plus 4-1 | Supports integrity, secure development, verification and controlled updates. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-066] |
| Restrict PLC/safety-controller exposure | **Restricted Data Flow; zones and conduits** | Limits paths from enterprise, cloud, vendor or HMI zones to control assets. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-067] |
| Generate evidence of intervention | **Timely Response to Events plus audit mechanisms** | Supports detection/event evidence; the MR itself establishes the safety-related evidence requirement. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-068] |
| Resist network/resource disruption | **Resource Availability** | Complements the MR §1.2.6 safe-behaviour requirement under network interruption. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-069] |
| Secure controller/product development | **62443-4-1** | Secure-development lifecycle, verification, defect and patch management. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-070] |
| Secure PLC/HMI/gateway components | **62443-4-2** | Component-level requirements for embedded, host, network and software components. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-071] |
| Secure OEM/integrator remote-service processes | **62443-2-4** | Security-program requirements for IACS service providers. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-072] |

| Operate and maintain the installed machine securely | **62443-2-1** | Asset-owner security management and lifecycle governance. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-073] |

: Mapping Machinery Regulation concerns to relevant IEC 62443 engineering layers. {#tbl-iec62443-mapping}

The seven 62443 foundational requirement families—identification and authentication control, use control, system integrity, data confidentiality, restricted data flow, timely response to events and resource availability—are useful, but their relevance to machinery safety is not symmetrical. **Integrity, authentication, use control, restricted data flow, event evidence and availability often have direct cyber-physical significance; confidentiality may be essential under other legislation yet have little machinery-safety significance unless loss of confidentiality enables or contributes to a hazardous attack.** [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-074]

### Reference architecture

A defensible connected-machine architecture can therefore look like this:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-connected-machine-reference-architecture
%%| fig-cap: "Reference zoning for a connected industrial machine, separating remote service, edge/DMZ, engineering, control, safety and plant OT functions."
%%| fig-alt: "A layered architecture in which vendor remote service reaches the machine through authenticated remote access and a machine DMZ or edge layer; HMI and engineering functions reach the machine control zone through controlled access; the machine safety zone has a constrained interface to the control zone; plant SCADA and MES connect through an OT firewall; cloud analytics receives outbound telemetry."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart TB
    V[Vendor Remote Service]
    R[Remote Access Gateway]
    D[Machine DMZ / Industrial Edge]
    E[HMI / Engineering Zone]
    C[Machine Control Zone<br/>PLC / CNC / robot / VFD]
    S[Machine Safety Zone<br/>Safety PLC / safe I/O<br/>safe drive functions / interlocks]
    F[Plant OT Firewall]
    P[Plant SCADA / MES]
    A[Cloud Analytics]

    V -->|MFA + VPN / TLS| R
    R --> D
    D -->|controlled management| E
    E -->|jump / access control| C
    C -->|constrained interface| S
    P --> F
    F --> C
    D -->|outbound telemetry| A
```

This is not a topology prescribed by the Regulation. It is an engineering derivation from the requirement to prevent connected devices, intentional corruption and malicious external influence from producing hazards, using IEC 62443's zones-and-conduits approach. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-075]

The key principle is:

> **Connectivity should not automatically confer control authority.**

An OPC UA session used to read production counts does not inherently need to write speed limits. A cloud analytics service used for predictive maintenance does not inherently need PLC-programming authority. An OEM maintenance tunnel does not inherently need permanent access to a safety PLC. A MES recipe service does not inherently need the right to overwrite the parameters that delimit a validated safe-motion function.

That is **least privilege applied to physical causality**: grant a digital system only the degree of machine authority required for its function.

The safety zone should consequently have a particularly narrow trust boundary. Depending on the machine and risk assessment, reasonable measures include separate engineering roles, cryptographically protected configuration where supported, validated parameter ranges, physical/local enabling for especially sensitive maintenance actions, configuration hashes or signed baselines, monitored access and independently enforced safe-motion constraints. These are engineering measures, not verbatim Annex III requirements. Their justification is the need to prevent corruption or malicious access from invalidating the safety function. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-076]

### Remote access is remote authority

**Remote access deserves special treatment because it collapses geography without reducing authority.** An engineer thousands of kilometres away can, depending on implementation, possess the same logical privileges as a person connected locally to the engineering port. Annex III does not say “use MFA” or “use a jump host”; it says the connected/remote path must not lead to hazardous situations and safety-related systems must withstand the relevant malicious attempts. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-077]

A sound remote-maintenance sequence is therefore:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-remote-maintenance-control-sequence
%%| fig-cap: "Derived control sequence for privileged remote maintenance."
%%| fig-alt: "A sequence beginning with deny by default, followed by authenticated request, site or operator authorisation, a time-bounded least-privilege session routed through a controlled gateway or jump point, monitored and attributable actions, separate authorisation for safety-sensitive changes, session termination, automatic revocation and retained evidence."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[Deny by default] --> B[Authenticated request]
    B --> C[Site / operator authorisation]
    C --> D[Time-bounded session]
    D --> E[Least privilege]
    E --> F[Controlled gateway / jump point]
    F --> G[Monitored and attributable actions]
    G --> H[Separate authorisation for safety-sensitive changes]
    H --> I[Session termination]
    I --> J[Automatic revocation]
    J --> K[Retained evidence]
```

MFA, individual accounts, plant-controlled gateways, temporary credentials, session recording, firewall rules and explicit maintenance windows are **derived controls**. They become compelling where the threat model shows that stolen or abused remote credentials could produce the hazardous states covered by Annex III §§1.1.9 or 1.2.1. IEC 62443-2-4, 3-2 and 3-3 provide useful engineering structure for this reasoning. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-078]

Permanent vendor VPNs, shared “service” accounts and remote-desktop products installed directly on HMIs are not automatically prohibited by the Machinery Regulation. But if they create an inadequately protected path to compliance-critical software or a reasonably foreseeable malicious route to dangerous motion, the manufacturer needs to explain how the EHSRs are nevertheless satisfied. “The customer requested TeamViewer” is not, by itself, a safety argument.

### Standards landscape

The standards landscape as of September 2026 can therefore be characterised as follows:

| Standard / family | Role | Machinery Regulation status as of 23 Sep 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| **ISO 12100:2010** | Machinery risk assessment/risk reduction. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-079] | Foundational machinery-safety reference; exact MR harmonisation list still pending. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-080] |
| **ISO 13849-1:2023** | Safety-related control-system design, including software. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-081] | Important functional-safety standard; future MR OJ status must be checked when list publishes. |
| **ISO 13849-2** | Validation of safety-related control systems. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-082] | Functional-safety validation, not general cybersecurity. |
| **IEC 62061:2021, incl. current amendments** | Machinery functional safety of safety-related control systems. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-083] | Functional-safety framework; not a complete security framework. |
| **IEC 61508 series** | Generic functional-safety basis for E/E/PE safety-related systems. | Generic rather than machinery-specific; IEC 62061 is the machinery-sector application. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-084] |
| **IEC TS 63074:2023** | Security aspects related to machinery functional safety. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-085] | Highly relevant bridge document; a Technical Specification, not itself a blanket harmonised-MR route. |
| **IEC 62443 series** | IACS cybersecurity across product, system, service-provider and asset-owner lifecycle. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-086] | Powerful engineering reference, **not mandated by MR**. |
| **prEN 50742:2025** | Machinery — Protection against corruption. | Draft as of September 2026; not yet a final harmonised MR standard. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-087] |
| **ISO/IEC 27001** | Organisational information-security management | Useful organisationally but not a machine/product-safety conformity route. |
| **ETSI EN 303 645** | Consumer-IoT security reference | Not a general Machinery Regulation compliance standard. |
| **EN 18031 family** | Cybersecurity standardisation in another EU product-law context | It should not be assumed to confer Machinery Regulation conformity; applicability depends on the separate product regime involved. |

: Standards relevant to machinery safety, functional safety and cybersecurity, with their status as of 23 September 2026. {#tbl-standards-landscape}

The broader point is important: **harmonised-standard status is legal metadata, not a property intrinsic to a technically good standard**. A technically excellent IEC 62443 implementation can provide strong evidence but does not acquire presumption of conformity until the applicable EU legal mechanism says that it does. The Commission's current machinery page is explicit that the first Regulation-specific harmonised list is still forthcoming. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-088]

## AI, the Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2: one machine, multiple legal lenses

### AI and autonomous behaviour

The digital-regulatory picture changed materially again in July 2026. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744—the **Digital Omnibus on AI**—entered into force on **27 July 2026** and amended both the AI Act and Regulation 2023/1230. The Commission's current AI Act page confirms that high-risk AI rules for systems embedded in regulated Annex I products now have an extended transition to **2 August 2028** and that the amendment was designed in part to clarify interaction between the AI Act and product-safety legislation, particularly the Machinery Regulation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-089]

The amendment is particularly relevant to machinery. It adds to Machinery Regulation Article 8 a delegation requiring the Commission to amend Annex III with health and safety requirements for AI systems classified as high-risk under the AI Act because they are safety components of machinery or themselves covered products, reflecting the relevant AI Act requirements; those delegated acts are to apply by **2 August 2028**. It also adds a transitional presumption-of-conformity bridge in Article 20 for relevant AI standards/common specifications. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-090]

This does **not** mean that machinery has no AI requirements until 2028. Regulation 2023/1230 already contains machinery-specific obligations concerning fully or partially self-evolving behaviour, varying autonomy, safety-function limits and records of safety-related software decisions; Annex I also specifically addresses ML-based safety-function categories for conformity assessment. Those machinery provisions apply with the Regulation's main regime from 20 January 2027. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-091]

Nor should four distinct technologies be conflated:

| Technology | Machinery analysis |
|---|---|
| **Deterministic PLC logic** | Ordinary automation; still subject to software integrity and cyber-safety requirements when compromise can create hazards. |
| **Adaptive controller** | May become relevant to the self-evolving requirements if operating rules/behaviour change during operation; safety limits must remain bounded. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-092] |
| **Machine-learning safety function** | Explicitly important under the Machinery Regulation's high-risk/conformity-assessment architecture and potentially the AI Act product-safety regime. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-093] |
| **Generative AI** | Not automatically a machinery safety component. Its legal significance depends on what it does. A chatbot describing maintenance manuals is fundamentally different from an AI agent authorised to generate and execute motion commands. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-094] |

: Distinguishing deterministic automation, adaptive control, machine learning and generative AI in machinery analysis. {#tbl-ai-technology-distinction}

### The Cyber Resilience Act

The next layer is the **Cyber Resilience Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/2847**. The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. Its main product obligations apply from **11 December 2027**, while its reporting obligations apply from **11 September 2026**—meaning that, as of the date of this research, the CRA reporting regime has already begun. The Commission characterises the CRA as imposing mandatory cybersecurity requirements across the planning, design, development and maintenance of products with digital elements, including vulnerability handling throughout their lifecycle. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-095]

That timing creates a notable overlap:

**11 September 2026 — CRA vulnerability/incident reporting starts**  
**20 January 2027 — Machinery Regulation main requirements, including Annex III cyber-safety, apply**  
**11 December 2027 — CRA main product cybersecurity requirements apply**  
**2 August 2028 — revised high-risk AI product timetable / machinery AI integration point**

[^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-096]

The two product regulations solve different problems.

| Lens | Core question | Typical obligations |
|---|---|---|
| **Machinery Regulation** | Can the machine cause injury or other covered harm, including because digital systems are corrupted or maliciously manipulated? | Risk reduction, EHSRs, safe control systems, protection against corruption, safety-software identification/logging, safe network-failure behaviour. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-097] |
| **Cyber Resilience Act** | Is the product with digital elements sufficiently cyber-resilient throughout its supported lifecycle? | Cyber risk assessment, secure design/default, vulnerability handling, security updates, vulnerability reporting, technical documentation and CRA conformity assessment. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-098] |
| **NIS2** | Is the organisation operating its network and information systems with adequate cybersecurity risk management and incident resilience? | Entity-level risk-management measures, incident handling, continuity, supply-chain security, vulnerability management, access security and MFA where appropriate. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-099] |
| **AI Act/MR AI layer** | Does safety-relevant AI meet the specific risk-management, data, technical, oversight and product-safety requirements applicable to high-risk AI? | AI-specific requirements according to classification and current transition timetable, increasingly integrated with sectoral product legislation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-100] |

: Four regulatory lenses that may apply simultaneously to a connected industrial machine. {#tbl-regulatory-lenses}

A connected industrial machine can readily be a CRA **product with digital elements** when its intended or reasonably foreseeable use involves a direct or indirect data connection. Its embedded PLC/HMI software, update mechanism and vulnerabilities then matter even where a particular vulnerability would never generate a machinery hazard. The CRA addresses the larger product cybersecurity envelope; the Machinery Regulation narrows its cyber inquiry around health-and-safety consequences. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-101]

The intersection is the important part:

**vulnerability → exploit → control-system compromise → unsafe physical state**

At that point the same technical defect can matter under both laws.

For example, an unauthenticated PLC firmware-update endpoint is a CRA problem because it is a cybersecurity weakness in a digital product. If exploiting it allows safety-critical behaviour to be changed so that a person can be injured, it is also a Machinery Regulation issue under Annex III §§1.1.9/1.2.1. The CRA itself recognises that its cybersecurity requirements and those of the Machinery Regulation can address similar cybersecurity risks; the regimes should therefore be engineered coherently rather than as unrelated compliance projects. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-102]

The CRA additionally brings lifecycle mechanisms that the Machinery Regulation does not specify at the same level: vulnerability handling, security-update responsibilities, reporting and support-period responsibilities. Its vulnerability-handling requirements also make software-component knowledge and SBOM-type practices much more directly relevant. The CRA should thus become the **product-security lifecycle layer**, while Machinery Regulation analysis determines which of those security properties also form part of the safety case. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-103]

### NIS2 and the plant operator

**NIS2 sits somewhere else again.** Directive (EU) 2022/2555 regulates entities and their network/information-system risk, not CE conformity of an individual machine. Article 21 covers such matters as risk-analysis policies, incident handling, business continuity, supply-chain security, secure acquisition/development/maintenance, vulnerability handling, cyber hygiene, access control and, where appropriate, multi-factor authentication. NIS2 also reaches manufacturing categories through its annexes, so a machinery manufacturer or plant operator may itself be an essential or important entity depending on sector, size and applicable national transposition. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-104]

This gives a useful first-principles model:

**Machinery Regulation → protect the person from hazardous machine behaviour**

**CRA → protect the digital product and its users against cybersecurity risk**

**NIS2 → protect the organisation and its network/information systems**

**AI Act / MR AI provisions → control risks specific to qualifying AI systems**

They overlap technically, but they are not interchangeable legally.

## Lifecycle compliance: procurement, FAT/SAT, updates and substantial modification

The largest implementation mistake would be to treat Annex III §§1.1.9 and 1.2.1 as a cybersecurity feature to be added immediately before CE marking. The requirements touch architecture, component selection, development, integration, commissioning, maintenance and future updates. IEC 62443 reinforces this lifecycle view through the distinct responsibilities of product suppliers, system integrators/service providers and asset owners. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-105]

### Procurement requirements

For procurement, requirements should therefore be classified according to their actual legal basis rather than all being labelled “Machinery Regulation requirements”.

**Legend:** **MR-E** = explicit Machinery Regulation requirement; **MR-D** = derived engineering measure supporting an MR safety requirement; **CRA** = Cyber Resilience Act requirement/supporting implementation; **62443** = IEC 62443 engineering practice; **OWNER** = purchaser/asset-owner contractual requirement.

| Procurement requirement | Proper classification | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Inventory of safety-relevant software/firmware versions | **MR-E + CRA** | MR requires identification of software necessary for safe operation; CRA reinforces component/vulnerability lifecycle management. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-106] |
| SBOM in machine-readable form | **CRA / OWNER**, not a standalone MR mandate | Useful for vulnerability/component management; MR requires identification/protection of safety-relevant software but does not simply say “provide an SBOM”. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-107] |
| Secure configuration baseline | **MR-D + 62443 + CRA** | Demonstrates which configuration constitutes the validated machine state. |
| Unique named privileged accounts | **MR-D + 62443** | Supports attribution and prevention of unauthorised modification; MR states the safety outcome, not account syntax. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-108] |
| RBAC / least privilege | **MR-D + 62443** | Limits who can change safety/control state. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-109] |
| MFA for remote privileged access | **MR-D + 62443 + NIS2 where applicable + OWNER** | Strong response to credential-based remote attack; not literally prescribed by MR. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-110] |
| Disable unused services/ports | **MR-D + CRA + 62443** | Reduces paths capable of compromising compliance-critical assets. |
| Cryptographically protected/signed updates | **MR-D + CRA + 62443** | Strong implementation for preventing intentional software corruption and securing product updates. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-111] |
| Vulnerability-management process | **CRA + 62443**, and **MR-D** where vulnerabilities affect safety | CRA explicitly establishes lifecycle vulnerability responsibilities. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-112] |
| Patch policy and maximum remediation windows | **CRA + OWNER**; safety impact assessed under MR | CRA creates product-security lifecycle duties; purchaser should convert them into contractual service levels. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-113] |
| Plant-controlled remote-access gateway | **MR-D + 62443 + OWNER** | Limits the authority of remote paths; topology itself is not legally prescribed. |
| Complete network-interface and protocol documentation | **OWNER + MR-D + 62443** | Needed to establish attack surface and validate conduits. |
| Firewall / segmentation requirements | **MR-D + 62443** | Derived from threat model and restricted-data-flow design. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-114] |
| Safety/control logging and modification evidence | **MR-E** for the safety-related evidence required by Annex III, expanded by **62443/OWNER** | The Regulation expressly requires intervention/configuration evidence and safety-software traceability. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-115] |
| Time synchronisation | **62443 / OWNER / MR-D** | Makes distributed evidence attributable and reconstructable; not an explicit MR requirement by itself. |
| Backup and tested restore of PLC/HMI/safety configurations | **62443 + NIS2/OWNER + MR-D** | Supports recovery and known-good restoration. |
| Coordinated vulnerability-disclosure contact | **CRA + OWNER** | Part of a mature vulnerability-handling lifecycle. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-116] |
| Support lifetime / end-of-support declaration | **CRA + OWNER** | Cyber support horizon affects whether the machine can be operated securely over its physical life. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-117] |
| Notification before safety-relevant firmware becomes unsupported | **OWNER + MR-D** | Prevents an asset owner unknowingly depending on an unmaintainable safety-security component. |

: Procurement requirements classified by legal or engineering basis. {#tbl-procurement-requirements}

For machinery with twenty-year physical lives, the final two rows are strategic. The useful mechanical lifetime of a press, packaging line or robot cell can greatly exceed the support life of an embedded operating system, VPN appliance or industrial PC. The CRA makes security support a product-lifecycle issue; the Machinery Regulation makes obsolete digital components a safety concern whenever their vulnerabilities can compromise the protective functions on which the safety case depends. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-118]

### FAT/SAT and commissioning

**FAT and SAT therefore need a cybersecurity extension.** Traditional FAT proves that the machine performs and that its safety functions operate under designed test conditions. For a connected machine after 20 January 2027, acceptance should also generate evidence that relevant digital attack or failure paths do not invalidate those functions.

| FAT/SAT test family | Example evidence | Regulatory/engineering purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity and access** | User/account list, privilege matrix, default-account test, failed-login tests, remote MFA test | Demonstrate controlled access to compliance-critical software. Annex III §1.1.9 plus IEC 62443 IAC/UC. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-119] |
| **Network exposure** | Port/service scan, firewall rules, machine data-flow diagram, approved OPC UA methods/tags | Demonstrate that conduits correspond to intended functionality. |
| **Software baseline** | PLC/safety-PLC program hash, firmware versions, HMI version, drive firmware, signed baseline | Supports §1.1.9 software identity and intervention evidence. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-120] |
| **Safety configuration** | Safety parameter export, checksum, PL/SIL validation references, access-control test | Demonstrates that cyber controls protect the same configuration validated by functional safety. |
| **Remote maintenance** | Test of default-deny state, authorisation, MFA, timeout, revocation and audit trail | Validates the highest-risk external control conduit. |
| **Logging and traceability** | Successful/failed programming-event records, user attribution, configuration-change records | Directly supports MR evidence requirements. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-121] |
| **Communication failure** | Disconnect/reconnect Ethernet, loss of OPC UA/MES/cloud link, malformed/stale input test where justified | Demonstrates Annex III §1.2.6 safe behaviour. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-122] |
| **Unauthorised change attempt** | Rejected PLC/safety parameter upload, firmware-integrity rejection, alarm/log evidence | Tests protection against intentional corruption. |
| **Backup/restore** | Restore from trusted backup followed by safety-validation check | Demonstrates recoverability to known configuration. |
| **Update process** | Authenticity validation, controlled installation, rollback/recovery and post-update verification | Links CRA lifecycle practice to preservation of the MR safety case. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-123] |

: Cybersecurity extensions to machinery FAT/SAT and the evidence they can generate. {#tbl-fat-sat-tests}

FAT/SAT cyber evidence should not be viewed merely as an IT appendix. Where the manufacturer relies on those controls to satisfy Annex III, the evidence belongs in the conformity rationale and should be traceable to the technical documentation, risk assessment, architecture and verification records. Annex IV's ability to reach safety-related software/programming logic underscores that software evidence is now part of the conformity domain. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-124]

The same reasoning has to survive commissioning:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-machinery-digital-lifecycle
%%| fig-cap: "Machinery lifecycle from design through operational change and decommissioning."
%%| fig-alt: "A left-to-right lifecycle from design, manufacture and integration through FAT, SAT, commissioning, operation and maintenance, then patching, firmware or software update, functional modification, safety modification, possible substantial modification and decommissioning."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[Design] --> B[Manufacture] --> C[Integration] --> D[FAT] --> E[SAT]
    E --> F[Commissioning] --> G[Operation] --> H[Maintenance]
    H --> I[Patch] --> J[Firmware / software update]
    J --> K[Functional modification] --> L[Safety modification]
    L --> M[Possible substantial modification] --> N[Decommissioning]
```

### Updates and substantial modification after commissioning

The difficult point is the boundary between maintenance and a legally substantial modification. A usable decision logic is:

**Was the change foreseen or planned by the original manufacturer?**

If yes, that weighs strongly against Article 3(16), although implementation still has to preserve conformity.

**Does the change create a new hazard or increase an existing risk?**

If no, the substantial-modification definition is not satisfied merely because code changed.

**If safety is affected, does the modification meet the remaining Article 3(16) threshold concerning required guards/protective devices and safety-control modification, or additional protective measures for stability/mechanical strength?**

Only if the complete definition is met should Article 18's “modifier becomes manufacturer” consequence be triggered. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-125]

This is why a critical CVE patch and a new production mode should not be processed identically. A validated security patch can preserve the manufacturer's original safety envelope. A “small PLC change” that defeats an interlock can transform the risk model even if the binary file changes by only a few bytes.

Nor does the existing CE marking answer the question. **CE marking describes conformity of the product placed on the market under its applicable assessment; it is not an immutable property of every future configuration.** If a later modification satisfies Article 3(16), the person making it assumes manufacturer obligations under Article 18 for the affected machinery/product and the conformity question reopens accordingly. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-126]

## Case study, critical answers and the boundary of cyber-physical safety

### Conventional architecture and attack paths

Consider a robotic palletising/packaging cell containing a standard PLC, safety PLC, HMI, Ethernet-connected variable-frequency drives, robot controller, safe I/O and guard interlocks. The machine exchanges production data with SCADA/MES through OPC UA. The OEM maintains it remotely through an Internet-connected gateway, and an industrial edge computer sends telemetry to a cloud predictive-maintenance service.

A conventional architecture might place the HMI, PLC, robot, drives, safety controller and remote gateway on a largely flat machine network. The vendor tunnel is permanently available, PLC programming is possible from an engineering laptop or HMI, MES can write recipes, and the cloud edge has broad access because that was operationally convenient.

The machine can still achieve a calculated PL or SIL when tested against random hardware failures. But the architecture has introduced new common-cause paths that the PL/SIL number does not represent.

#### Attack path A: remote maintenance

A vendor account is stolen. The attacker enters through the remote gateway, reaches the engineering interface, uploads modified PLC logic, alters a mode transition and causes the robot to start when the original sequence would have required a local reset.

Security failure: credential/control-path compromise.

Safety failure: unexpected hazardous motion.

Regulatory path: Annex III §1.1.9 because the remote connection enables hazardous behaviour and software is intentionally modified; §1.2.1 because a reasonably foreseeable malicious third-party attempt can lead to a hazardous situation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-127]

#### Attack path B: safety-parameter manipulation

An engineering station is compromised. The attacker obtains access to the safety PLC and changes the permissible speed in a reduced-speed maintenance mode from the validated value to a much higher one.

The safety function has not “failed” in the traditional random-failure sense: it faithfully enforces the maliciously changed parameter. Yet the risk reduction has disappeared.

That is exactly why §1.1.9's configuration/software integrity and §1.2.1's safety-function limits are consequential. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-128]

#### Attack path C: cloud-to-control authority

A cloud-service credential or edge device is compromised. Because the edge computer has write access to controller tags, the attacker manipulates recipe or motion parameters.

The engineering mistake is not cloud connectivity per se. It is allowing an analytical service's compromise to cross directly into **machine control authority**.

### Redesigned architecture

The redesigned architecture therefore treats authority, not connectivity, as the scarce resource:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-case-study-redesigned-machine-architecture
%%| fig-cap: "Redesigned case-study architecture in which remote service, plant OT and cloud analytics do not automatically obtain machine control authority."
%%| fig-alt: "OEM service reaches a default-off, time-bounded remote-access gateway through per-user MFA and a plant-approved VPN, then a jump host and HMI or engineering zone. The machine DMZ mediates OPC UA and edge functions. Plant SCADA and MES connect through an OT firewall. The control zone has a strictly constrained interface to the safety zone. Cloud analytics receives outbound telemetry from the edge and has no direct PLC or safety-PLC control path."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart TB
    O[OEM Service]
    R[Remote Access Gateway<br/>default off / time boxed]
    J[Jump Host]
    H[HMI / Engineering]
    D[Machine DMZ<br/>OPC UA / edge broker]
    P[Plant SCADA / MES]
    F[OT Firewall]
    C[Control Zone<br/>PLC / robot / drives]
    S[Safety Zone<br/>safety PLC / safe I/O<br/>interlocks / safe motion]
    A[Cloud analytics]

    O -->|MFA + per-user ID<br/>plant-approved VPN| R
    R --> J
    J --> H
    H -->|controlled programming| C
    P --> F
    F --> D
    D -->|read-oriented flows| C
    C -->|strictly constrained safety interface| S
    D -->|outbound telemetry only| A
```

This architecture does not pretend that a firewall is a safety device. Instead, it ensures that compromise of a non-safety digital service does not automatically confer authority over the safety state. The actual safety functions remain engineered and validated through ISO 13849/IEC 62061 methods; segmentation, authentication, software integrity and access controls protect the assumptions under which those functions remain valid. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-129]

The remote gateway is normally disabled or logically closed; vendor access requires named authentication, site authorisation and a limited session. Safety-controller programming can require a higher privilege level and, where the risk justifies it, a local physical maintenance condition. Machine telemetry can cross outward to analytics, while return traffic is either absent or mediated through a narrow application interface. Changes to safety software/configuration produce attributable evidence. Communications loss leads to a defined safe or otherwise non-hazardous behaviour consistent with §1.2.6. These controls are derived designs; the statutory requirements remain the safety outcomes in Annex III. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-130]

### Critical questions

The principal questions can now be answered directly.

| Question | Evidence-based answer |
|---|---|
| **Does Regulation 2023/1230 impose cybersecurity requirements?** | **Yes.** Annex III §1.1.9 expressly requires protection against intentional corruption, and §1.2.1 expressly addresses reasonably foreseeable malicious attempts by third parties leading to hazardous situations. The Commission itself describes the Regulation as integrating cyber-safety provisions. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-131] |
| **Which cybersecurity requirements are explicit?** | Protection of compliance-critical hardware/software/data against intentional corruption; safety-relevant software identification; intervention/modification evidence; resistance of control systems to relevant foreseeable malicious attempts; safety-function limits; safety-software/change traceability; and safe behaviour under network-connection failure are explicit. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-132] |
| **Which controls are indirect engineering consequences?** | MFA, firewalls, zones/conduits, jump hosts, signed firmware, secure boot, allowlisting, IDS, session recording and particular RBAC models are not named by MR. They can be justified as engineering means to meet its objectives. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-133] |
| **Is IEC 62443 mandatory?** | **No.** It is a highly relevant engineering framework, not a statutory requirement of the MR. As of 23 September 2026 the first MR harmonised-standard list is still pending. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-134] |
| **Can a cyber vulnerability make a functionally safe machine non-compliant?** | **Yes, conditionally.** If the vulnerability means compliance-critical assets are inadequately protected or a reasonably foreseeable malicious path can lead to a hazardous situation, satisfying a PL/SIL target does not cure the Annex III non-conformity. Not every vulnerability has that safety consequence. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-135] |
| **Can a software update constitute a substantial modification?** | **Yes.** Article 3(16) explicitly includes digital modifications, but the full statutory test must be satisfied; a software update is not automatically substantial. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-136] |
| **Who is responsible when an integrator substantially modifies machine software?** | Article 18 can treat the natural/legal person carrying out the substantial modification as the manufacturer for the purposes of the Regulation. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-137] |
| **How should manufacturers treat remote vendor access?** | As a communication/control path within the machinery threat and risk model. Where it can influence hazardous behaviour, its authentication, authorisation, scope, duration, monitoring and ability to reach safety-critical assets require justification. The exact technical solution is not prescribed. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-138] |
| **Does an original CE marking automatically remain sufficient after significant software modification?** | **No general safe-harbour exists merely because the machine was once CE marked.** Apply the Article 3(16) test. A substantial modification invokes Article 18 manufacturer obligations; a non-substantial update still has to preserve conformity. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-139] |
| **Must intentional cyber manipulation enter the machinery risk assessment?** | Where a malicious manipulation is reasonably foreseeable and can lead to a hazardous situation, §1.2.1 makes the answer effectively **yes** for that safety pathway. The risk analysis should connect the threat to the hazardous machine state rather than conduct an unrelated enterprise-IT assessment. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-140] |
| **How do CRA and Machinery Regulation interact?** | CRA supplies horizontal product-cybersecurity lifecycle duties; MR addresses machinery health-and-safety consequences. The same weakness can violate both when exploitation creates unsafe physical behaviour, but compliance with one should not be assumed automatically to discharge the other except where EU law creates a specific presumption/equivalence mechanism. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-141] |
| **What changes for manufacturers on 20 January 2027?** | Machinery newly placed on the EU market moves to the Regulation's regime: new definitions and economic-operator framework, Annex I conformity-assessment architecture, explicit substantial-modification rules, digital-documentation provisions, and the new software, corruption, malicious-attempt, network and self-evolving-system EHSRs become operative. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-142] |

: Critical questions and evidence-based answers concerning the Machinery Regulation's digital and cyber-physical implications. {#tbl-critical-questions}

### From machine safety to cyber-physical safety

The central proposition can therefore be tested rather than merely asserted.

**Fact:** Regulation 2023/1230 expressly protects compliance-critical hardware, software and data against intentional corruption; requires evidence of software/configuration intervention; requires relevant control systems to withstand foreseeable malicious third-party attempts capable of creating hazards; and introduces explicit network-failure and self-evolving-system requirements. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-143]

**Regulatory implication:** A safety case can no longer stop at proving that the safety PLC, interlock or drive reaches its required PL/SIL under the traditional failure model if digital paths exist through which those safeguards can foreseeably be intentionally altered or defeated.

**Engineering implication:** Threat modelling, software integrity, privileged-access control, architecture, remote-access security and traceability become inputs to machinery-safety engineering whenever they protect assumptions necessary for risk reduction. IEC TS 63074 and IEC 62443 provide technically credible bridges for doing this. [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-144]

**Interpretation:** This is correctly described as a movement from **machine safety toward cyber-physical safety**. The Regulation does not make cybersecurity and safety identical; it removes the artificial boundary between them where digital compromise can cause physical harm.

**Recommendation:** Manufacturers should stop organising the work as “Safety does CE; IT does cybersecurity”. The more defensible engineering model is a single causal assurance chain:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-integrated-safety-security-assurance-chain
%%| fig-cap: "Integrated assurance chain linking machinery hazards, safety functions, digital dependencies, threat modelling, security requirements and lifecycle evidence."
%%| fig-alt: "A left-to-right assurance chain from hazard analysis to safety functions, then their digital dependencies, a threat model against those dependencies, derived security requirements, machine architecture, combined safety and security verification, a software and configuration baseline, FAT and SAT evidence, and controlled lifecycle change."
%%| fig-align: center
%%{init: {"theme": "neo", "look": "handDrawn", "layout": "elk"}}%%
flowchart LR
    A[Hazard analysis] --> B[Safety functions]
    B --> C[Digital dependencies<br/>of safety functions]
    C --> D[Threat model]
    D --> E[Security requirements]
    E --> F[Machine architecture]
    F --> G[Safety / security verification]
    G --> H[Software / configuration baseline]
    H --> I[FAT / SAT evidence]
    I --> J[Controlled lifecycle change]
```

That model is more than regulatory housekeeping. It follows directly from the physical reality of modern machinery: **once software and communications can alter motion, force, speed, sequencing, protective logic or the authority to command them, the integrity of the digital control system becomes one of the conditions under which the machine remains physically safe.** [^eu-machinery-regulation-2023-1230-cyber-physical-safety-source-145]
